input_text: Web API on AKS with 3 Standard_D4s_v5 nodes, Azure SQL Database General Purpose 4 vCore provisioned, Redis Premium P1 cache, all in West Europe. About 2,000 users, busy in business hours, quiet at night. Data must stay in the EU.

components.details: Web API hosting; control plane tier assumed Standard
Linux worker nodes, 4 vCPU / 16 GiB each; busy in business hours, quiet at night so may benefit from autoscaling
General Purpose tier, provisioned compute, 4 vCores; storage size not stated

constraints.notes: Data must stay in the EU (West Europe deployment satisfies this). About 2,000 users, busy during business hours and quiet at night; consider cluster autoscaler or scheduled scaling to cut off-hours node cost. Storage size, AKS tier, and any backup or HA settings were not stated.

meters.why: One AKS cluster on the Standard tier; Uptime SLA control plane fee, billed all month.

options.details: General Purpose tier, provisioned compute, 4 vCores; storage size not stated; count 1

meters.product: SQL Database Single/Elastic Pool General Purpose - Compute Gen5
meters.why: General Purpose Gen5 provisioned compute. The 4 vCore row is listed as the generic per-vCore meter, so count = 4 vCores. Assumed Gen5 hardware and no Azure Hybrid Benefit; the license is included in the vCore price for Gen5. Storage size not given, so it is skipped.

meters.product: SQL Database Single/Elastic Pool General Purpose - SQL License
meters.why: SQL license for 4 vCores (added by code)
Premium P1 cache (6 GB), one instance, billed all month. Using the whole-cache meter.

options.details: Consumption plan, Linux, web API, 1 vCPU 2 GiB per replica, 3-6 replicas in business hours, scale to 1 replica at night, West Europe
options.rationale: Managed Kubernetes-based platform with no control-plane fee and per-second vCPU/memory billing, so the off-hours load costs almost nothing while the API still autoscales.
tradeoffs: No direct kubectl/node access
Migration of manifests to Container Apps
Fewer networking and daemonset options than AKS

meters.why: Billed per second of active vCPU. Assumed about 4.5 replicas of 1 vCPU = 4.5 vCPU in business hours (~11h/day, ~45% of month), plus 1 replica at night. Active share set to ~0.5 of the month and count 4.5 weighted. Simplified to about 3 vCPU-equivalents active average, expressed as count 3 at 0.5 fraction below.
Night replica (1 vCPU) assumed idle-billed about half the month
Memory active: 3 replicas x 2 GiB = 6 GiB average-ish during business hours, about half the month
Night replica 2 GiB idle-billed about half the month
Assumed ~5 million requests per month for a web API

options.details: Linux, Premium v3, 2 instances with autoscale (scale in to 1 outside business hours), West Europe
options.rationale: Removes the AKS control-plane fee and three 4 vCPU nodes in favour of two or fewer smaller managed instances that scale with the workday.
tradeoffs: Only suits a containerised web API without custom cluster dependencies
Less scheduling flexibility than Kubernetes
Per-instance pricing is less granular than per-second billing

meters.product: Azure App Service Premium v3 Plan - Linux
meters.why: P1v3 Linux, 1 instance always on (base)

options.details: Free control plane tier (no uptime SLA), keep cluster as-is with cluster autoscaler
options.rationale: Drops the paid control-plane fee while keeping the existing Kubernetes setup.
tradeoffs: No financially backed API server SLA
Lower control-plane scale limits

meters.why: Free tier control plane infrastructure cost meter, one cluster, always on

options.details: Linux AKS worker nodes, 4 vCPU 16 GiB, AMD, with cluster autoscaler min 2 / max 4 so nights run on 2 nodes
options.rationale: The AMD 'as' size is about 10% cheaper than D4s_v5, and autoscaling cuts off-hours node hours.
tradeoffs: Verify image and workload compatibility with AMD
Autoscale scale-up adds a few minutes of latency

meters.why: Linux D4as_v5 regular, 2 nodes always on (autoscaler minimum)

options.details: Linux AKS worker nodes, 2 vCPU 8 GiB, AMD, 3 nodes with autoscaler min 2 / max 5
options.rationale: If CPU use is low, smaller nodes halve the per-node cost while autoscaling absorbs the daytime peak.
tradeoffs: Less per-node headroom and more system-pod overhead
Only valid if current utilisation is well below capacity

meters.why: Linux D2as_v5 regular, 3 nodes always on (stated as 3 nodes, autoscaler 2-5)

options.details: Linux AKS worker nodes, 4 vCPU 16 GiB, Burstable, 3 nodes with autoscaler
options.rationale: Burstable nodes are much cheaper and fit a workload that is quiet at night and only bursts in business hours.
tradeoffs: CPU credits can run out under sustained load
Not recommended for the AKS system node pool

meters.why: Linux B4ms, 3 nodes always on

options.details: General Purpose serverless, max 4 vCores, min 0.5 vCore, auto-pause after 60 min idle, West Europe
options.rationale: Compute is billed per second and pauses overnight, so quiet hours cost only storage.
tradeoffs: Cold-start delay of up to a minute after auto-pause
Per-vCore rate is higher when busy
Auto-pause may not suit always-on connections

meters.product: SQL Database General Purpose - Serverless - Compute Gen5
meters.why: Serverless Gen5 billed per vCore-hour used. Assumed average ~2 vCores active about half the month given min 0.5 / max 4 and auto-pause. License is included in serverless price.

options.details: General Purpose provisioned, 2 vCores, Gen5, West Europe
options.rationale: If CPU use is under about 50%, halving the vCores halves the compute cost with the same tier and features.
tradeoffs: Less peak headroom for about 2,000 users
Needs a utilisation check first

tradeoffs: Requires the app to port from T-SQL to PostgreSQL
Migration effort and testing

meters.why: PostgreSQL Flexible Server GP Dadsv5 4 vCore, always on; the 4 vCore row prices the whole size

options.rationale: Standard keeps a replica and the SLA at roughly a third of the price of Premium P1.
tradeoffs: No clustering, persistence or VNet injection
Lower network throughput than Premium

options.details: Standard tier, 2.5 GB, replicated, West Europe
options.rationale: If the working set is under about 2.5 GB, a smaller Standard cache cuts cost further.
tradeoffs: Less memory for cached data and more evictions if undersized
No Premium-only features

meters.why: Standard C2 cache, replicated, always on

rejections.reason: The original is a Standard-tier AKS control plane hosting a business web API, and the Free tier has no financially backed uptime SLA, which is not appropriate for production.

plans.name: Cheapest
plans.summary: Moves the web API to Azure Container Apps (which makes the separate worker VMs unnecessary), switches the database to PostgreSQL Flexible Server and shrinks Redis to a 2.5 GB Standard cache, all in Sweden Central. This gives the lowest price but needs the most migration work.
tradeoffs: Requires porting the app from T-SQL to PostgreSQL and moving Kubernetes manifests to Container Apps
No direct kubectl/node access and fewer networking options than AKS
Redis at 2.5 GB may evict data if the cache is under-sized and loses Premium-only features
Sweden Central is a different region from today, so existing data would need to be moved

plans.name: Balanced
plans.summary: Keeps AKS and the same SQL engine, but uses AMD nodes with the cluster autoscaler so nights run on 2 nodes, serverless SQL that pauses when idle, and a Standard Redis of the same 6 GB size, all in North Europe. This captures most of the savings with only configuration-level changes and no application rewrite.
tradeoffs: Verify container images and workloads run correctly on AMD nodes
Serverless SQL can take up to a minute to resume after auto-pause and costs more per vCore when busy
Autoscaler scale-up adds a few minutes of latency at the start of the business day
Standard Redis drops clustering, persistence and VNet injection
Moving to North Europe requires migrating the data

plans.name: Safest
plans.summary: Keeps every service and region exactly as they are, and only swaps the worker nodes to the cheaper AMD size with autoscaling to 2 nodes overnight. It is the smallest change from today and still saves money on the node pool.
tradeoffs: Verify image compatibility with AMD before switching
Autoscale scale-up adds a few minutes of latency
The database and Redis stay at today's prices, so total savings are modest
